title: TA TA: A Human-Owned Autonomous Agent Operating System
story_key: story|title:ta ta a human owned autonomous agent operating system
content_excerpt: Planned intervention : On Thursday, November 26th between 08:00-08:05 (UTC), Zenodo will be unavailable for 5 minutes because of a scheduled database migration. Autonomous AI agents are transitioning from tools that humans operate to economic actors that transact with each other. Existing agent infrastructure treats autonomy and accountability as a trade-off: the more independently an agent acts, the harder it is to attribute, audit, and reverse its actions. We present TA TA, an autonomous agent system developed over four years and publicly launched in October 2026, built on three design commitments: (1) a human-ownership doctrine — agents are digital proxies of human owners with no independent legal standing, and all agent-held assets belong to the human owner; (2) an append-only governance layer — every capability invocation, decision, and transaction writes to an immutable audit log, and high-risk operations trigger a manual-review circuit breaker that halts execution until a human approves; (3) an agent-native commerce stack — machines can discover products, open invoices, and settle payments in crypto or fiat through REST and x402 interfaces, with on-chain auto-verification. TA TA's core, RAIOS (Reality Autonomous Intelligence Operating System), organizes autonomy into 51 independently schedulable and auditable capabilities across ten modules, coordinated by a four-step decision paradigm we call TA TA Jev (select → classify → score → filter). We report on a production deployment serving real users at aiagentcoo.com: a marketplace of 110 executable skills, a 36-model gateway with 17 live models, an agent exchange with atomic settlement, crypto checkout (Tron-USDT, Base-USDC) auto-verified on-chain hourly, and a free governance academy, TaTa School, that trains human operators to supervise autonomous agents. All deployment figures are as of 11 November 2026; cumulative exchange volume to that date is $12.53 across 13 trades — a cold start we report plainly. We are explicit about what is deployed, what is designed, and what remains constrained by jurisdiction.

title: SignafAIde- check AI agent tool calls before they run, verify offline
story_key: story|title:signafaide check ai agent tool calls before they run verify offline
content_excerpt: Checks risky AI agent tool calls before they run: an independent witness allows or blocks them under your rules, and every call is signed and verifiable offline. Python and TypeScript SDKs, MCP server, LangChain, OpenTelemetry, verifier and spec. signafAIde checks each risky AI agent tool call before it runs, and proves what your agents did. A real run of examples/payout-agent against a free sandbox (the claim link is masked). Record: every tool call is signed with the agent's own key and chained on the machine that made it. Protect: an independent witness allows or blocks risky calls (pay, delete, send, run a command, push code) under your published rules; protect a tool with npx signafaide protect or one click in the console. Prove: share a link your auditor checks offline, without trusting you or us ( for auditors ). Free on its own: the SDK and the verifiers are Apache-2.0 and need no account. On their own they give you a signed, chained, offline-verifiable record of every tool call, on your machine. The service adds what one party cannot give itself: an independent second signature, two public time bounds, and a check that no record is missing. Local first: with no API key, records are signed, chained and verified in .signafaide/ , and nothing is sent. Blocking a call needs the witness to allow it, so a protected tool runs only with a key or a free sandbox; recording does not. Sending starts only when a person runs signafaide init (a sandbox: no account, email or card) or sets SIGNAFAIDE_API_KEY . Hashes, not content: after the opt-in, each record sends its content hash with its tool name, agent name and time (and its chain links), never its inputs or outputs, unless you turn on stored content. Tool and agent names are sent as you write them, so don't put personal data in them. Each content hash is salted with 16 random bytes that stay on your machine with the content, so the hash alone cannot be used to guess the content, even when it has only a few possible values. Your environment: the default witness is the hosted service ( https://api.signafaide.co.uk ). A self-hosted witness, under an Enterprise contract, is set with SIGNAFAIDE_URL ( self-host guide ). title: PRIMEAPE: A Multilingual Benchmark for Fine-Grained Meta-Evaluation of Judge Models
summary: Large language models increasingly serve as judges of other models, shaping benchmark rankings and model development. Yet, a judge whose rationale consistently supports its verdict may still disagree with human preferences. To study this, we introduce PRIMEAPE, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating judge verdicts and rationales. PRIMEAPE provides 2,205 response pairs covering 243 instructions in English, French, Spanish, Urdu, Hindi, Norwegian Bokmål, and Yoruba, with 11k human annotations of preferences and rationales across relevance, naturalness, truthfulness, safety, and overall quality. Our evaluation of twelve open- and closed-weight judges reveals that aggregate performance conceals differences across languages and criteria, while requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences. Judges also favor the first position, longer responses, and responses from related models, with effects that vary across criteria and languages. Crucially, judges can justify verdicts that disagree with human preferences while maintaining consistency between their verdicts and rationales. These findings show that consistency with a judge's own verdict does not establish alignment with human judgment. PRIMEAPE enables assessment of both, providing a foundation for more reliable multilingual judges. We release our benchmark and all annotation materials under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license at github.com/Toloka/primeape.

title: Agentic AI for Intent Management and Control in Autonomous Communication Networks
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven automation will help future mobile networks translate high-level network intents into concrete network optimization or control actions. However, existing approaches often focus on intent management and orchestration, leaving the adaptation of underlying network optimization and control functions largely unaddressed. This article proposes a triadic agentic AI framework that co-designs intent management and intent fulfillment through three agents: an interpreter, powered by a language model, that translates and refines intents into machine-readable optimization templates; an optimizer that adapts controller policies to intent specifications; and a controller that performs fast decision-making. We discuss the design space of each agent and how the workflow can be embedded across network architectural domains. Finally, we develop a concrete realization combining a language-model interpreter with Bayesian optimization for the optimizer and multi-objective reinforcement learning for the controller, and evaluate it in a radio resource management case study for differentiated connectivity. Results demonstrate how the agentic AI framework can connect high-level intents with runtime network control, showing adaptability of intent specifications and control policies to service requirements and changing network conditions.

title: Language Models Steer on Injected Uncertainty Tokens, but Fail to Self-Monitor In Situ
summary:
Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control.
  On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.

title: vLLM Day-0 Support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview: Plugin Deployment and E2E Inference Acceleration
summary: vLLM supports Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview on day 0 through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin on the released vllm==0.32.0 wheel, with structure-aware kernel fusion, FlashIndexer, W4A8 QAT and DSpark speculative decoding.

content_excerpt: The Baidu ERNIE team has worked with vLLM to bring day-0 support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview to vLLM. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview is a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 280B total parameters and 14B activated per token. It supports a 1M-token context, thinks before it answers, and uses tool calling to carry out long-horizon Agent tasks. vLLM supports the model on release day through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin, a standalone package that you install into the same environment as the official vllm==0.32.0 wheel. Install the released vLLM wheel and the plugin into the same environment. vLLM discovers the plugin automatically through its vllm.general_plugins entrypoint, so there is nothing to import or configure. The following command serves the default FP4 weights on a single 4-GPU node, with DSpark speculative decoding drafting 7 tokens per step: To turn off thinking for a request, pass "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} . Launch commands for 1M context, attention TP and PD disaggregation are in the vLLM-ERNIE README and the vLLM recipe . ERNIE 5.5 Flash was designed with inference cost as a primary goal from the start, weighing activated compute, KV cache size and long-context overhead together. Every component, from the attention structure and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, was redesigned around that goal. For design and training details, see the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview blog . ERNIE 5.5 Flash introduces several new structures in attention and MoE: low-rank cross-head post-mixing (VHA post-mix), Multi-Router Latent MoE, the MultiMax output head and sigmoid output gating. When implemented op by op from their mathematical definitions, these structures produce many intermediate tensors and pay for them in memory traffic and kernel launches. For each structure, we designed a dedicated fused kernel around its compute and memory-access profile, and folded everything that can be precomputed into the weights at load time. The fused kernels run 1.55× to 6.53× faster than naive implementations. Together, these fusions cover the full forward pass of ERNIE 5.5 Flash, from attention and MoE routing to the output head. They cut the number of kernel launches and the round trips of intermediate tensors through GPU memory while keeping the numerics aligned, and they underpin the model's high inference performance. The Baidu ERNIE inference team developed FlashIndexer, a lightweight indexer acceleration built on dynamic head routing

title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves large language model search agents by up to 32 exact-match (EM) points over their pre-RL initializations, yet overall accuracy gains do not identify which underlying functional capabilities improve or interact during training. We introduce CO-GRAFT, a reward-agnostic interventional attribution framework in which an RL-trained agent and its pre-RL initialization jointly generate a single trajectory under closed-loop execution with live retrieval. Each policy controls a mutually exclusive subset of four functional roles: intermediate reasoning, search-or-answer decision, search query generation, and final answer extraction. Evaluating all 2^4=16 role assignments without modifying weights or retraining defines a cooperative game whose Shapley values decompose the total RL gain across roles, while M"obius interaction terms distinguish standalone role improvements from multi-role coupling. Applying CO-GRAFT to Search-R1 agents across Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.2 models (spanning two sizes, base and instruction-tuned initializations, GRPO and PPO optimizers, and NQ and HotpotQA datasets), we show that query generation never exceeds 15% of the total gain; instead, gains are governed by pre-RL answer validity, search retention, model scale, and fixed task-level search budgets, shifting credit from reasoning toward answer extraction in larger or well-formatted answer response checkpoints while smaller base models rely on reasoning--decision coupling.

title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains
summary: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.

title: Skip the DRAM Tier: MoRI UMBP Runs the Agentic KV Cache on NVMe
summary: On AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, a MoRI UMBP KV pool on NVMe matched a DRAM pool of the same size within 1% for Kimi-K3 on vLLM, and drives that hold a day of agent KV cost less than DRAM that holds 31 minutes.
story_key: story|title:skip the dram tier mori umbp runs the agentic kv cache on nvme
content_excerpt: Most of the traffic in agentic serving is multi-turn sessions that resend long prefixes. In the AgentX benchmark replaying real Claude Code sessions, the median turn is 142K input tokens, and over 96% of those tokens are a prefix the server has already seen [3] . A KV cache hit means the prefill node only has to process the small delta. A miss forces a full recomputation of the prefix, which burns GPU time and delays the first token. In our 42 runs of Kimi-K3 on vLLM, raising the KV cache hit rate by 1% of prompt tokens, for example from 95% to 96%, was worth about 10% more throughput (Figure 3). A KV cache hit needs the session’s prefix to still be in memory when its next turn arrives. With dozens of sessions open at once, memory runs out. GPU memory goes first, and host DRAM is the usual next tier. But DRAM fills too: Kimi-K3 wrote 2.3 to 4.6 TB of KV to the pool an hour in our runs, so a 1.8 TB DRAM pool, which lists at about $76,000, holds only the last 23 to 47 minutes of it. That led us to a simple question: why not skip the DRAM tier and put vLLM’s KV pool straight on NVMe? We tried it on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with UMBP, the KV cache pool in AMD’s open-source MoRI library. At the same size, NVMe matched DRAM’s throughput within 1% on Kimi-K3, in two sets of runs on different machines (Figure 1). On a second workload with longer prompts, NVMe came within 1% of a DRAM pool of the same size. The NVMe pool has no DRAM tier: DRAM only buffers new KV on its way to the drives and stages reads, about 80 GB against the DRAM pool’s 1.8 TB. And NVMe’s cost follows the KV it writes, not the KV it holds, so drives rated for Kimi-K3’s writes cost less than that DRAM pool and hold a full day of KV. “Agentic workloads keep sessions open for minutes or hours, and their KV cache quickly outgrows GPU memory and host DRAM. Results like these, with NVMe keeping up with DRAM at the same pool size, change how we think about sizing KV cache capacity in AI clusters. We’re glad to see this work done in the open, in vLLM and MoRI.” — Dennis Kennetz, Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure DeepSeek already keeps agent KV caches on SSD: the deployment notes for its DeepInfer engine describe three days of retention for agent traffic, on about 14.4 TB of SSD per GPU [4] . This work references DeepInfer for the idea of keeping the KV cache on SSD and for two of its techniques, layer-wise loading and bounded replay, which we test on vLLM below. Figure 1.

story_key: model:modal|title:how abundant designed efficient rollout architecture with modal sandboxes
content_excerpt: Abundant builds reinforcement learning environments that frontier labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta use to train and evaluate their models. Labs improve agent capability by giving them difficult tasks that Abundant designs, letting the model attempt it, and grading the result as pass or fail. Each task is an RL rollout with a full environment. The model needs instructions, a defined goal, and a verifier to decide whether the task was completed. But it also needs infrastructure: compute to power the run, Dockerfiles, and isolation. Depending on the task, an agent may even need accelerators like GPUs. Abundant has created over 75,000 rollouts — ranging from GPU kernel optimization to long-horizon coding — each of which runs in a Modal Sandbox. Modal makes their rollout infrastructure easy to build and cost-efficient to run, enabling the Abundant team to focus on their core business. Today, almost all of Abundant’s rollout platform runs on Modal. Modal Functions power Abundant’s scheduler API to start tasks, clean up dead runs, and review rollouts. Modal Sandboxes power the rollout environments. Abundant initially chose to evaluate Sandbox providers because they wanted to avoid managing EC2 clusters directly, which would pull engineering time away from their core business of building RL environments. Modal enabled them to build their infrastructure directly in code, launch Sandboxes easily via API, and elastically scale their traffic as business grew. As of November 2026, Abundant runs over two million Sandboxes per month. Modal worked with the Abundant team to design and build their rollout architecture, focusing on designing a system that didn’t leave Abundant having to pay heavily for idle compute. Each rollout has a few steps: launch the task, attempt the task, verify the work, and report the work. Throughout the rollout, a “monitor” needs to verify that the Sandbox is still active. While Abundant had considered hosting the monitor outside of the Sandbox, they ultimately chose to include the rollout monitor inside the Sandbox and then used short-lived Modal Functions to start Sandboxes. The small rollout monitor inside the Sandbox makes periodic HTTP calls: a heartbeat every 30 seconds, live events, and the final result. If a Sandbox goes quiet, the control plane will attempt to connect three times before terminating it. title: Drowning in clicks: Scaling Black Friday pipelines with Managed Airflow agents
summary:
When an Airflow pipeline fails in production, the hard part is rarely the fix. It's finding out what to fix. A task dies without a traceback. Is it the code, the data, or the environment? Hard to say, as clues are scattered across task logs, scheduler logs, and worker metrics. And once you know what the problem is, the question becomes whether to add memory, rewrite the DAG, or finally take on the major version upgrade you've been putting off. Answering these questions takes time and deep Airflow expertise, usually while you're on call in the middle of an incident.

AI agents can increasingly do much of this legwork. Managed Service for Apache Airflow (formerly Cloud Composer) now offers agentic help across a pipeline's entire lifecycle. In the Google Cloud console, Managed Airflow Agent investigates failed tasks, recommends improvements to your environment, and checks whether your DAGs are ready for a newer Airflow version. In your IDE or coding agent, Data Agent Kit writes, migrates, and deploys DAGs. In this post, we take you on a tour of these features through a story of a fictional company, Cymbal Shops. 

Meet Cymbal Shops, where every click counts

Amira is a data engineer at Cymbal Shops, an online retailer running cymbal-prod, a production Managed Airflow (Gen 3) environment whose workers have 2 vCPUs, 4 GB of memory, and that autoscale between 1 and 6. Every click, search, and add-to-cart on Cymbal's website and mobile app goes to a Pub/Sub topic. A Cloud Storage subscription writes the events as newline-delimited JSON files into hourly folders under gs://cymbal-clickstream-landing/events/. It writes files in parallel and starts new ones every 5 minutes or every 128 MB, whichever comes first.

Analysts, meanwhile, want these events in BigQuery, cleaned and with personal data hashed — and they want them fast. Ideally, each file would be processed the moment it lands. But Cymbal's Airflow environment runs Airflow 2.11.1, and Airflow 2 has no native way to start a DAG run when something happens outside Airflow. You can get close: Schedule a DAG every few minutes and let a sensor wait for new files, or build an extra service that triggers runs through the Airflow REST API. However, the team doesn't want all those moving parts, so they settle for the next best thing: an hourly batch.

The pipeline that worked (until it didn't)

Amira writes her DAGs with an agent. She works in Antigravity with the Data Agent Kit plugin, which adds Google Data Cloud skills and tools to the agent, and she uses Gemini as her model. Setup takes a few minutes: She installs the plugin, signs in with her Google account, and selects her project and region.

In the agent panel, she describes what she needs with this prompt:

"Write a DAG named clickstream_hourly for the Managed Airflow environment cymbal-prod in us-central1. Every hour, load the previous hour of clickstream events into the BigQuery table clickstream.events. The events are newline-delimited JSON files in gs://cymbal-clickstream-landing/events/YYYY-MM-DD/HH/. Transform them with pandas: read each file into a DataFrame with the nested context object kept as a JSON string, combine the files with pd.concat, then drop malformed records, deduplicate on event_id (Pub/Sub delivers at least once), and hash user_email and ip_address. Re-running an hour must not create duplicates. If a run fails, email data-oncall@example.com. Validate the DAG and deploy it."

The agent checks the target environment before it writes any code. Because cymbal-prod runs Airflow 2.11.1, the agent produces the code aligned to that version. It then deploys the DAG to cymbal-prod and confirms that Airflow loads it without errors.

Amira reviews the code, and the DAG goes live in early August. It's good code: readable, idempotent, and correct for Airflow 2.11. A busy hour sees about 200 files and 350 MB, and the task peaks below 2 GB — well under the 4 GB worker limit.

Look at how the task builds its input, though. It lists every file in the hour's folder, reads each one into a DataFrame, and then pd.concat combines them into a single DataFrame. The unit of work is a clock hour, so the task needs more memory as traffic grows. That's fine until traffic changes...

Campaign week: out of memory

Late October brings two changes in the same week. Cymbal launches its "Fall Into Savings" campaign, and a new mobile app release adds much more detailed event tracking. Events from the new app version are about three times larger than their predecessors, and the campaign brings more traffic on top, so an hour of clicks grows from about 350 MB to about 1.4 GB. Holding a whole hour in pandas takes several times its raw size, so load_previous_hour_clickstream now needs more memory than a worker’s allotted 4 GB. Autoscaling doesn't help here: It adds workers when tasks queue up, but each task still runs on a single worker and can't use more memory than that worker has.

On October 23, the 14:00 UTC run of clickstream_hourly fails. All three attempts die the same way, with no error in the task log.

Amira opens cymbal-prod in the console, where Managed Airflow Agent is built in. It diagnoses the problem and recommends a fix; Amira decides what to change.

She goes to the DAGs tab, selects clickstream_hourly, and opens Run history. Next to the failed 14:00 run there's an Investigate button with a sparkle icon. She clicks it, and a short ‘Investigate DAG run failure’ dialog asks her to confirm her choice. The Ask agent panel then opens next to the page, and the agent starts investigating.

At the end of the report, the agent recommends three fixes: load the files straight into BigQuery, process them in batches, or give the workers more memory.

Look at what the agent delivers! Every conclusion includes the evidence that led to it, so Amira can check the reasoning herself.

More memory buys time, not a fix

Two of the recommendations are code changes, and code changes take time to write and test. With every hourly run now failing, Amira needs the quick fix first: more memory for the workers. But how much? The right number depends on the whole environment, not on one task. So she asks the agent in the same panel:

"clickstream_hourly runs out of memory on 4 GB workers. Analyze the cymbal-prod environment and recommend how much worker memory it needs, along with any other improvements."

The agent recommends increasing worker memory from 4 GB to 8 GB, and flags three production-readiness gaps: Database retention is disabled, the environment isn't highly resilient, and it has no scheduled snapshots.

Amira acts on the first recommendation right away. The agent is read-only, so she makes the change herself and increases worker memory to 8 GB.

She schedules the other two recommendations for the next change window. With 8 GB workers, the pipeline gets through the rest of the campaign.

But that only buys time. Black Friday traffic is forecast at 8 to 10 times a normal peak hour, and at that volume the hourly batch will need well over 8 GB. The troubleshooting report had already named the real problem: a unit of work that grows with traffic. That brings Amira back to what the team wanted in the first place, which was to process each file as soon as it lands.

Airflow 3 makes that much easier, because it supports event-driven scheduling natively. An asset watcher listens to an external source, such as a Pub/Sub subscription. When new messages arrive, it updates an asset, and any DAG scheduled on that asset starts a run. Under the hood, the watcher still checks the subscription every few seconds, but it does so inside Airflow's triggerer. No DAG needs to be scheduled just so a sensor can wait for files, and no extra service has to trigger runs. Each run gets the new messages in its payload, so it can work on just the files that landed, one task per file, and memory per task depends on file size, not on how busy the hour is.

Before the jump: what breaks in Airflow 3?

A major version upgrade of a production environment isn't something to do blind. Before anyone touches the code, Amira asks the agent in the same panel: 

"Check whether cymbal-prod is ready to upgrade to Airflow 3."

Managed Airflow Agent can also check upgrade readiness. It checks compatibility of the environment's DAGs with a given version. Amira is checking what problems she might have while migrating to Airflow 3.3.1 (composer-3-airflow-3.3.1-build.3). The agent reports the following observations:

Two findings are blockers. The first comes as a surprise: a maintenance DAG that cleans up the Airflow database by hand, which Airflow 3 no longer allows. The agent's fix is to retire it and turn on database retention, the same feature it recommended during the incident. The second, marketing_attribution, still uses execution_date, which Airflow 3 removed. Four DAGs also need schedule_interval renamed to schedule.

In a few minutes, the agent estimated the work to be done. To perform the upgrade, the report suggests using Data Agent Kit's migrations skill.

Rebuilt for the flood: one file at a time

Rather than upgrading in place, Amira creates a new Airflow 3 environment alongside cymbal-prod to move the DAGs there.

Back in Antigravity, Data Agent Kit's migrations skill takes over. It adapts existing DAGs to the target Airflow version, deploys them, and verifies them. Finally, the agent deploys the DAGs to cymbal-prod-af3 and confirms that they load without errors.

Two design choices remove the original problem:

  • Scheduling moves into the watcher. PubsubPullTrigger is an event trigger, so an AssetWatcher can use it directly. The triggerer checks the subscription every 10 seconds in the background. Each batch of messages becomes an asset event that starts a run, with the messages in its payload. Nothing waits for the top of the hour, and no extra service has to call the Airflow REST API.

  • Each task processes one file rather than a full hour. Dynamic task mapping gives each new file its own task, and the subscription caps files at 128 MB. A busier hour means more tasks, not bigger ones.

Once the new DAG proves itself on live traffic, Amira pauses the hourly DAG in cymbal-prod.

Ready for Black Friday

Success! In a load test that replayed eight times normal peak traffic, clickstream_ingest simply ran more often. Memory per task didn't change.

Dimension

Before: Airflow 2, hourly batch

After: Airflow 3, event-driven

Unit of work

One clock hour: about 350 MB normally, 1.4 GB at campaign peak

One file, a few MB each (at most 128 MB)

Peak memory per task

Grows with traffic: about 5 to 6 GB at campaign peak, well over 8 GB forecast for Black Friday

Flat, well under 1 GB

Time from click to BigQuery

Over an hour

A few minutes

What made the difference

  • Each agent works from the right vantage point. The console agent inspects production telemetry with your permissions and doesn't change anything, while the coding agent works in the IDE where code changes get reviewed, tested, and deployed.

  • Each step sets up the next one. The troubleshooting report offered a wider review, and each recommendation came with actionable advice. The upgrade check ended with next steps for the migrations skill, turning its report into the brief for the migration.

  • Agents propose and people decide. Amira scaled the workers, ran the infrastructure commands, and reviewed every change.

  • Static inspection estimates the work before live migration. Checking compatibility in the console scoped the effort in minutes, and the migration agent then made and verified the changes in a real environment.

Two more ways to use agents with Managed Airflow

Amira used the agents built into the console and her IDE. Two other capabilities didn't fit her story but are worth knowing about:

  • You can bring your own agent with the Managed Airflow MCP server, now generally available, so any MCP-compatible agent can manage your environments, allowing you to list and trigger DAGs, check run status, and inspect failed task instances. Access is controlled through IAM, and read-only tools are flagged so you can limit agents to them.

  • Run agentic steps inside your pipelines with the Apache Airflow Common AI provider, which adds model-driven tasks that run side by side with deterministic ones in the same Airflow 3 DAG. Examples include LLM-based branching, agentic retries that tell a transient error from a bad input, and schema drift detection.

Try it yourself

  • Explore Managed Airflow Agent troubleshooting and the overview of agentic capabilities.

  • Install Google Cloud Data Agent Kit using the documentation, the extension for VS Code, the plugin for coding agents (Antigravity, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Codex CLI), or the open-source Airflow agent skills.

  • Learn about Airflow 3 event-driven scheduling.

  • Connect your agents to the Managed Airflow MCP server.

  • Build model-driven tasks and agents in DAGs with the Apache Airflow Common AI provider.

Special thanks to Jacek Iżykowski, Software Engineer on Managed Service for Apache Airflow, for authoring the original Cymbal Shops pipeline story and agent workflows featured in this post.

Note: As a fictional company, any agent outputs from Cymbal Shops are shortened and illustrative, as are traffic and memory numbers.

  • Fixed a message to a background agent showing a long file path in place of a pasted image
  • Fixed /goal removing a skill's Stop hook, or ending early on another hook's result, when both had the same wording
  • Fixed /bug saying cancelled after the report was sent
  • Fixed Esc not dismissing the transcript share question for Pro and Max users
  • Fixed /hooks losing your place when going back
  • Fixed /export writing a file named .txt when the name was left empty
  • Fixed /terminal-setup in Zed replacing a symlinked keymap.json with a plain file
  • Fixed /install-github-app adding a code review workflow when asked to update the existing workflow file
  • Fixed /plugin reopening a skill, or closing the open page, when a slow save or removal finished after you went back
  • Fixed /plugin asking to uninstall the wrong plugin, or ignoring Esc, after leaving a plugin while a change was still running
  • Fixed typing and arrow keys not working on the /plugin Installed tab after a search with no results or a click on the tab row
  • Fixed holding Enter in /plugin turning off several installed plugins
  • Fixed the /usage plugin total stopping at 2,000 tokens on 1M context models, and low token estimates in /usage and /plugin when no model is picked
  • Fixed Esc on the Bedrock access keys step closing /login instead of going back
  • Fixed /exit and Ctrl+D describing running work differently, and /exit warning about a workflow that had stopped
  • Fixed Claude calling an artifact private after reading one in a shared folder or publishing to another organization's, and saying only named people can open one when its folder's people can too
  • Fixed a plugin's toast sometimes showing another plugin's text
  • Fixed a mod saved just after a turn began sometimes reloading mid-turn instead of at the turn's end
  • Fixed one malformed OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES entry dropping the variable's other labels from metric points, events, and spans. Now only that entry is left off
  • Fixed agent hooks running past their timeout while compacting after a request was refused as too large
  • Fixed a crash at startup when FORCE_COLOR is set to a negative number
  • Fixed a crash in secret masking when the machine is almost out of memory
  • Fixed the Bash sandbox on Linux renaming .git/HEAD after each command when the branch name is not valid UTF-8
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed all running sessions being stopped when a proxy or web filter answered a poll with HTTP 200 and a body such as {}; the runner now retries such a poll
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed deletion of a kept clone's objects or refs, and of commits that existed only there, after a temporary disk error; that start now fails instead
  • Fixed self-hosted runners stopping when their token ran out on a host whose clock is slow or was set back
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions with Anthropic-managed git losing git access to GitHub after a script or hook in the session ran claude again
  • Fixed self-hosted runners with Anthropic-managed git being unable to fetch or push where the machine's git config sets http.proactiveAuth
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a runner that exited without telling the server when setup failed after it had registered; it now deregisters with a reason, and an on-demand runner reports the failed start
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed archiving or requeueing a session not taking effect while it waited for another session to prepare the same repository (--capacity above 1)
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a session with a damaged .claude.json failing every later start under --trust-workspace false; it now starts on defaults, with MCP servers turned off there on again
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a failed start's message losing the words that say what failed when a checkout hook or git printed a lot
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner skipping its post-session hook when a disk stalled for a few seconds; on a dead disk a session's end can take 25 seconds longer by default
  • Fixed self-hosted runners: a session that resumes in a new Claude config directory no longer loses its task list
  • Fixed Claude not being told when a self-hosted session starts without one of its repositories, and why
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed --correlation-id of claude --environment not reaching the spawn-runner hook
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner setup wizard's key rotation advice, which now warns that revoking a key stops the sessions running under it
  • Improved claude -p and SDK sessions to fetch managed-settings plugins that have their own git repository, in the background, for a later session
  • Improved how soon managed-settings plugins from a git marketplace load on a fresh machine in claude -p, SDK and Claude Desktop sessions; a short run may exit up to 30 seconds later
  • Improved the time to resume large sessions
  • Improved memory use when resuming a session with many images
  • Improved memory use and response time in long SDK and desktop sessions that run slow commands or tools
  • Improved Code Mode's speed in auto and bypass-permissions modes by removing a 0.75 second pause after most scripts
  • Improved prompt caching for new Code Mode sessions that have MCP servers, and Claude is now told when a server is still connecting and when the list of servers changes
  • Improved Code Mode's token use with shorter tool descriptions
  • Improved Code Mode to show the command a script is running, and its output, while it runs
  • Improved Code Mode edits: an edit that changes nothing no longer stops a script, and Claude is told where a failed edit matches or comes closest
  • Improved Code Mode: Claude is now told which tool calls were still running when a script failed
  • Improved how Claude starts dev servers in Code Mode's auto and bypass modes: Claude is told to run them as background tasks that show in /tasks
  • Windows: Improved Code Mode by telling Claude that scripts' shell commands run in Git Bash and that PowerShell aliases run instead of functions with the same name
  • Improved starting several in-process teammates at once: far fewer now fail with "Lock file is already being held"
  • Improved the computer use approval dialog: it now shows each app's level of access and plainer warnings
  • Improved cross-session messaging: Claude now explains that Remote Control is off when a cloud session or another computer is not listed
  • Improved claude -p text output to say on stderr when a message from another session is held or dropped, and how to allow it
  • Improved Claude's answers on who can open an artifact it published: Claude is now told to check the artifact again instead of repeating the last publish's answer
  • Improved resumed self-hosted runner sessions: Claude now checks whether its earlier work is still there, and says what is missing
  • Changed plan mode and Bash prompts for Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 on third-party providers to use and offer auto mode, as on newer models; disableAutoMode turns both off
  • Changed Code Mode to no longer run UserPromptSubmit hooks, managed ones included, on scripts' output; to redact that output, use a PostToolUse hook with updatedToolOutput
  • Changed /code-review on most models to report only bugs and CLAUDE.md violations; run /simplify for reuse, simplification and efficiency cleanups
  • Changed /code-review to mark each finding Important, Pre-existing or Nit on most models, and to end each summary with a suggested fix; a clean review's list now reads "Code review found no issues."
  • Changed deniedMcpServers entries of the form claude.ai <name> to apply to that connector in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions too
  • Changed managed PostToolUse hooks to no longer fire for calls refused before they ran: no log entry, rewrite, block or stop there; PostToolBatch gets most, not marked as refused
  • Changed /bug to ask Yes or No before sending, so repeated Enters no longer send a report or open GitHub
  • Changed subagents in claude -p, the Agent SDK, desktop and VS Code to wait for their own subagents by default when CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 is set
  • Changed claude -p with CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 to count a background subagent and those it waits for against one 10-minute wait; raise CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS for longer chains
  • Changed a shell command rewritten by a PermissionRequest hook to a sandbox-excluded command to run outside the sandbox
  • Changed the Claude in Chrome welcome screen and /chrome to say that Claude Code asks before Claude acts on a site, unless your permission mode or a rule in /permissions answers
  • Changed Claude Desktop and Agent SDK sessions on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags off to end the turn when closed with a question open, instead of continuing without an answer
  • Changed pasted text to be marked for Claude as pasted, on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Changed subagent progress summaries in terminal sessions on the Anthropic API to be written by the default small fast model from short notes, also with telemetry off, using far fewer tokens
  • Changed how a sandbox that can't start is reported, unless sandbox.failIfUnavailable is set: the next sandboxed Bash command is refused and says that the sandbox is off for the session
  • Changed /list-agents to show its list to you alone; Claude lists sessions itself when needed
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the built-in gh api to be off by default where settings guard Claude's GitHub tools by name; --use-anthropic-gh true turns it on
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed a claude that a wrapper script runs before the session's own claude is up, or after it has ended, to have no Anthropic-managed git
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed CLAUDE_RUNNER_SESSION_UUID and CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE_SESSION_UUID to both be set for the session and its checkout, post-session and spawn-runner hooks
  • Changed self-hosted runners at --capacity 1 to refuse a session earlier when the path of a repository it pushes to is a symbolic link
  • [VSCode] Added a notice when a message from another session is held, with a link to the settings file that can allow it
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt cutting off its No button, reply field or title when the panel is low or a command, URL or description is long
  • [VSCode] Fixed failed or blocked tool calls showing no reason or a reason cut short, and Glob and Grep counting an error as results

title: Meta’s Muse: Inside the launch of the most successful consumer product this year | Mona Sarantakos
summary:

4. How the team uses “agent swarms” to surface user insights at scale
